article.overview: A terrain mapping camera is an imaging instrument whose main purpose is to measure the shape of the ground: its heights, slopes and surface relief. Most such cameras acquire overlapping images of the same terrain from different viewing angles, and software converts the pairs or triplets into a digital terrain model (DTM), a grid of elevations. The class is defined by purpose rather than by a single design. The examples in this article include a dedicated three-line stereo imager on India's Chandrayaan-1 orbiter [1][2], a slant-stereo Terrain Camera on Japan's SELENE (Kaguya) orbiter [5][6], stereo DTMs made from the Narrow Angle Cameras of NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter [8][10], a follow-on stereo imager on Chandrayaan-2 [3][4] and a topography camera on China's Chang'e-3 lander [13][14]. These instruments differ in geometry, status and evidence base, so their figures should not be compared as if they described one product.
article.description:
Terrain mapping depends on geometry. A single image records brightness but not how high each feature is. If the same area is imaged from two viewing angles, a feature appears shifted between the two images in proportion to its height. This shift, called parallax, can be matched across the pair so that the height is calculated. Some designs use three looks (forward, nadir and aft) so that matches can be checked. Others use two slanted telescopes, or a single camera that obtains the second angle on a later orbit.

Terrain cameras are usually panchromatic, meaning they record one broad visible band, because a wide band gives a strong signal and fine detail. The output is normally a set of stereo images plus a camera model, which is the geometric description of how each pixel maps to the ground. A DTM is then produced with photogrammetric or automated stereo-matching software [8][9]. The quality of the DTM depends on the ground resolution, the angle between views, the accuracy of the spacecraft's position and orientation, and the independent altimetry used to tie the model to a reference height system. For example, LRO's Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) profiles were used to register NAC DTMs [8], and LOLA ranging was one of the inputs to the SLDEM2013 global elevation mosaic built from Kaguya TC images [6].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications:
Terrain mapping cameras serve several connected scientific goals. ISRO describes the purpose of the Chandrayaan-2 TMC-2 as mapping the lunar surface in the panchromatic band and producing high-resolution topographic maps and digital elevation models [3][4]. The Chandrayaan-1 TMC was defined in pre-launch documentation as an instrument to map the topography of both the near and far sides of the Moon and to prepare a three-dimensional atlas with high spatial and elevation resolution of 5 m [1]. The applications described in the sources include:

- **Global and regional topography.** Stereo-derived elevation products allow landforms to be compared across large areas. The JAXA SLDEM2013 global elevation mosaic was built mainly from SELENE TC stereo images, supplemented by Multiband Imager stereo data and LRO LOLA laser ranging [6].
- **Geomorphology and surface processes.** A DTM describes crater rims, slopes, flows and other features. Henriksen et al. used NAC DTM mosaics to map a large viscous flow related to Orientale basin ejecta and to estimate its thickness and volume, which they report to exceed 300 m and 500 km³ respectively [8].
- **Slope statistics.** The same NAC study computed slope statistics from 81 highland and 31 mare DTMs, providing a quantitative description of slope distributions in those terrain types [8]. Such statistics are a general input to surface science and operations planning; this article does not recommend any location.
- **Combination with other instruments.** ISRO states that the Chandrayaan-1 TMC digital elevation model, combined with the Lunar Laser Ranging Instrument (LLRI), could improve existing knowledge of lunar topography [1].
article.operating_principle:
The operating principle is photogrammetric triangulation. Each detector element views a known direction, defined by the optics and by calibration. When two or more images observe the same ground point from different positions, the intersection of the viewing directions gives the point's three-dimensional position. Pushbroom cameras build an image one line at a time as the spacecraft moves, so the viewing geometry is set by the orbit and by the fixed angles of the detector lines.

The Chandrayaan-1 TMC images in pushbroom mode with three linear detectors looking forward (+25°), at nadir (0°) and aft (−25°) [1]. The Chandrayaan-2 TMC-2 is described as producing stereo triplets from fore, nadir and aft views [3][4]. The Kaguya TC uses two slanted telescopes for stereo imaging and is described as a push-broom imager with 10 m spatial resolution from 100 km altitude [5][7].

The LRO NAC is not a dedicated stereo system. Stereo pairs are acquired over two or more orbits using at least one off-nadir slew, and the DTMs are generated and registered to LOLA profiles [8]. A separate LROC product, the Special Data Record NAC Digital Terrain Map (SDNDTM), uses photometric stereo, in which two or more images under different illumination resolve slope and albedo; it is not a geometric stereo DTM [11].

The Chang'e-3 topography camera was a lander-mounted imager on a camera bar. Its stated role was to observe the landing area, track rover movement and image the lander and rover [13][14]. The sources accessed for this article do not establish a stereo or DTM role for it.
article.scientific_importance: Terrain information is needed to interpret almost every other lunar observation. Surface composition, crater ages, regolith thickness and geological contacts all depend on where features are and how steep they are. Images alone cannot give height; stereo products add that third dimension. Global stereo-based products such as SLDEM2013 made lunar topography available at a scale that was not previously possible [6]. JAXA states that the elevation accuracy of SLDEM2013 is "nearly 10 meters or better" and that no earlier whole-Moon dataset had reached this accuracy [6]. That accuracy statement is the publisher's own and has not been independently re-derived for this article. The NAC study reports that DTMs have relative vertical and horizontal precisions less than the DTM pixel scale of 2–5 m, and absolute accuracies better than the uncertainties of the LOLA profiles used for registration [8].

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a terrain mapping camera. The orbital examples differ in mission altitude, detector layout, spectral band and integration, and the lander example is a different class of imager with a different field-of-view definition. The table below contains only values that the cited sources state. Where a source does not publish a value, the table says "not publicly specified". Each value is tied to the named instrument. The table is intended to show what is published, not to rank the instruments.

examples.article_text:
Chandrayaan-1 Terrain Mapping Camera (TMC)

**Status: flown.** The Chandrayaan-1 orbiter was launched on 22 October 2008, and communication was lost on 29 August 2009 [2]. The TMC was an instrument on that orbiter. ISRO states that data from the TMC and other instruments were processed to Planetary Data System (PDS) standards for archival and dissemination [2].

**Published configuration.** The ISSDC payload document describes the TMC as a panchromatic stereo camera with 5 m spatial resolution and 20 km swath [1]. It images from 0.5 to 0.85 µm and uses three linear 4k-element detectors for fore, nadir and aft views, with fore and aft view angles of ±25° relative to nadir [1]. It uses a single refractive optic covering the three detectors and a Linear Active Pixel Sensor with an in-built digitizer, and the expected data rate is of the order of 50 Mbps [1]. The payload dimensions are 370 mm × 220 mm × 414 mm and the mass is 6.3 kg [1].

**Evidence limits.** The ISSDC document is pre-launch: it uses future-tense wording such as "will image", and it gives configuration values rather than in-flight measurements. It does not state the TMC's power. Its statement that the TMC is "in the panchromatic band" is a configuration statement; it is not a measured radiometric calibration. A secondary search summary gave a spectral range of 0.4–0.9 µm for an early TMC description, which was not verified against a primary document and is not used here [1].

examples.article_text:
SELENE (Kaguya) Terrain Camera (TC)

**Status: flown.** The TC was one of the instruments of the Lunar Imager/SpectroMeter (LISM) package on SELENE (Kaguya), alongside the Multiband Imager and the Spectral Profiler [5]. The page accessed lists the principal investigator as Jun'ichi Haruyama of JAXA/ISAS [5]. The mission-operations dates were not stated on the pages accessed, so this article does not give an operating period for the TC.

**Published configuration.** The JAXA equipment page describes two telescopes, one looking forward and one looking backward, each with a one-dimensional detector, operating as a push-broom imager [5]. It gives a bandpass of 420 nm width covering 0.43 to 0.85 µm, with fields of view of 22.4° in full mode, 19.3° in nominal mode and 9.65° in half mode [5]. The ODE data-product help page states that the TC is a push-broom imaging camera with a spatial resolution of 10 m from 100 km altitude, and that its stereoscopic observations are planned for middle solar elevation angles [7]. The stereo angle, mass and power are not stated on the pages accessed. A secondary search summary gave a stereo angle that did not match the other summaries, so no stereo angle is given here.

**Data product.** The JAXA DARTS release for SLDEM2013 states that the main source of the elevation mosaic is "high-resolution (10m/pixel) stereo-images of the Terrain Camera (TC) onboard SELENE", supplemented by Multiband Imager stereo images and LRO LOLA laser ranging [6]. The release does not state the SLDEM2013 grid spacing, so the 10 m figure refers to the source imagery, not to the elevation grid [6].

![Flight model of the SELENE (Kaguya) Terrain Camera.](https://selene.tksc.jaxa.jp/en/equipment/image/img_tc_002.jpg)

*JAXA SELENE TC page caption: "TC Flight model". Credit: JAXA. Source: [JAXA SELENE Terrain Camera (TC) equipment page](https://selene.tksc.jaxa.jp/en/equipment/tc_e.htm) [5]. Reuse conditions for JAXA website images were not verified for this article.*

examples.article_text:
Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Narrow Angle Cameras (LROC NAC) used for stereo DTMs

**Status: flown.** The LROC Narrow Angle Cameras (NAC-L and NAC-R) fly on NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, which was launched on 18 June 2009 and is listed as an active mission [12]. Unlike the TMC and TC examples, the NAC is an imaging camera that is also used for terrain production. It is included here because its stereo DTM capability is well documented, and it is not a dedicated terrain mapping instrument [8].

**Published configuration.** The LROC specifications page gives a pixel scale of 0.5 m per pixel at 50 km altitude, an instantaneous field of view of 10 µrad, an effective focal length of 700 mm, a Kodak KLI-5001G detector with 1 × 5,064 pixels, a field of view of 2.85° per NAC, a mass of 8.2 kg per NAC, and peak and average power of 9.3 W and 6.4 W per NAC [10]. The ground scale applies at 50 km altitude; the page does not give a different figure for other altitudes [10].

**Stereo DTM capability.** Henriksen et al. report that the NACs each provide 0.5 to 2.0 m scale images of the lunar surface and that, although not designed as a stereo system, LROC can acquire NAC stereo observations over two or more orbits using at least one off-nadir slew [8]. They report that DTMs are generated from stereo sets and registered to LOLA profiles, with absolute accuracies better than the uncertainties of the LOLA profiles and relative vertical and horizontal precisions less than the pixel scale of the DTMs (2–5 m) [8]. They analysed 81 highland and 31 mare DTMs [8].

**Photometric-stereo product.** The LROC SDNDTM is a separate product set, built from NAC images with appropriate illumination and viewing geometries. The ODE help page describes photometric stereo, using two or more images to resolve slope and albedo, and it gives no numeric resolution or vertical accuracy [11]. It states that the three images for photometric stereo must be co-registered to sub-pixel accuracy and that products are created on a best-effort basis [11].

examples.article_text:
Chandrayaan-2 Terrain Mapping Camera-2 (TMC-2)

**Status: described as on the Chandrayaan-2 orbiter.** ISRO describes TMC-2 as a miniature version of the Terrain Mapping Camera on Chandrayaan-1 and as a follow-on to it [3]. The ISRO payload page describes the TMC-2 data as collected from a 100 km lunar polar orbit [3]. The ISRO payload pages accessed for this article do not state the current operational status, and an ISRO "Initial Results" page on TMC-2 exists, but its contents were not verified in full. The orbiter's launch and operating dates were not verified for this article.

**Published configuration.** ISRO's payload page gives a panchromatic band of 0.5–0.8 µm, a spatial resolution of 5 m, a swath of 20 km, and operation from a 100 km orbit [3]. The page describes stereo triplets with fore, nadir and aft views [3]. The ISRO topographic mapping page states that the aim is high-resolution topographic maps and digital elevation models of the lunar surface [4]. Mass, power and detector details are not stated on the pages accessed. A catalogue-level abstract reported a reduction of more than 40% in mass and power relative to the Chandrayaan-1 TMC; this figure was not verified against a primary ISRO or Space Applications Centre document and is not used numerically here.

examples.article_text:
Chang'e-3 lander topography camera

**Status: flown on the Chang'e-3 lander.** The topography camera is one of the lander's main scientific payloads, according to a 2015 *Research in Astronomy and Astrophysics* paper by Zhao et al. [13]. The paper's abstract-level description, as indexed in search results, states that it was meant to obtain optical images of the lunar topography in the landing zone, track rover movement and image the lander and rover [13]. The full text of that paper was not accessed for this article (the DOI resolved to a bot-protection page), so the statements from it are abstract-level only.

**Published configuration.** The IAC-14 abstract by Dai (2014) describes the topography camera as a high-resolution colour CMOS camera on a camera bar on top of the Chang'e-3 lander. It states that the camera field of view is 2352 × 1728 pixels. Scientists use the images to map the landing area and search for rocks to study, and engineers use them to observe the Yutu rover [14]. The abstract does not state the ground sampling distance, mass, power or band, so none are given here. The full IAC paper is restricted to authorised access [14].

**Naming note.** Some sources use "Terrain Camera" (TC) for lunar orbiter imagery used in DTM production. These refer to different instruments, so the Chang'e-3 lander camera should not be confused with the SELENE TC in Example 2.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Dimensions are published only for the Chandrayaan-1 TMC (370 mm x 220 mm x 414 mm, pre-launch document). Other examples do not publish dimensions in the sources accessed, so no general dimension is stated. Terrain cameras span pushbroom optics with different look angles, and their sizes should not be compared directly.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Published masses: Chandrayaan-1 TMC 6.3 kg (pre-launch document); LRO NAC 8.2 kg per camera. Mass for SELENE TC, Chandrayaan-2 TMC-2 and Chang'e-3 topography camera is not publicly specified in the sources accessed.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Published power: LRO NAC peak 9.3 W and average 6.4 W per camera. Power for the other examples is not publicly specified in the sources accessed.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen:
Terrain cameras operate in vacuum, under strong thermal cycling and in a radiation environment. Orbital imagers must maintain stable optics, precise detector alignment and a known viewing geometry, because the DTM depends on how accurately each pixel's direction is known.

Viewing geometry and illumination limit when stereo products can be made. The SELENE TC plans stereo observations at middle solar elevation angles and single-eye observations at low solar angles (below 30°) [5]. For photometric stereo, the LROC SDNDTM page notes that there are few large shadows except in the early morning and late afternoon, and that roughly ±30° to ±70° latitude bands give the best lighting geometry for the product [11]. The NAC stereo approach depends on at least one off-nadir slew across two or more orbits [8].

Altitude determines ground scale. The LROC NAC gives 0.5 m per pixel at 50 km altitude [10], while the SELENE TC gives 10 m from 100 km altitude [7]. A change of orbit therefore changes the ground scale of the same camera.

Data handling is a significant requirement. The expected data rate for the Chandrayaan-1 TMC is of the order of 50 Mbps [1]. The Chang'e-3 camera's sources mention image handling only in general terms, so no requirement is stated for it here.
article.limitations:
A single image cannot provide elevation. Stereo or photometric geometry, orbit and attitude knowledge, and an independent height reference are all needed. The resolution of an image is not the same as the vertical accuracy or grid spacing of a derived DTM. The SELENE TC images have 10 m resolution, but the SLDEM2013 release does not state its grid spacing [6].

Vertical accuracy claims are publisher statements unless they are supported by a peer-reviewed analysis. The SLDEM2013 "nearly 10 meters or better" statement is from JAXA [6]. The NAC accuracy statement is from a peer-reviewed study that is tied to LOLA registration [8].

Each example is a different design and mission context. A value for one instrument should not be applied to another. Lander-mounted topography cameras observe a local area and cannot produce global mapping products on their own.

Stereo products may be affected by illumination, shadows, surface texture and matching errors. The NAC DTM study reports that highland slopes were steeper than previously reported and attributes that partly to targeting bias toward higher relief terrain [8].

transportation_and_deployment.overview:
The terrain mapping cameras described here are carried by orbiters, with one exception. The Chandrayaan-1 TMC, the SELENE TC, the LRO NAC and the Chandrayaan-2 TMC-2 are integrated into orbiter payloads, launched, transferred to the Moon, inserted into lunar orbit and then commissioned. For the orbiter examples, the relevant interfaces are spacecraft integration, mounting and alignment, thermal control, pointing knowledge, power and data handling, and orbit altitude. The Chandrayaan-1 mission operated at 100 km altitude and was changed to 200 km from May to August 2009 [2]. The Chandrayaan-2 TMC-2 is described as operating from a 100 km polar orbit [3]. The SELENE TC is described as operating at 100 km altitude [7].

The Chang'e-3 topography camera is a lander payload. It was mounted on a camera bar on top of the lander [14]. Its integration would require the lander's mechanical, power and data interfaces, and the camera's position on the bar determines its view of the surface and the rover. The sources accessed do not provide the lander-side interface dimensions, mass allocation or data-handling details.
transportation_process: Integrate the camera (mounted with its electronics and alignment) onto an orbiter or lander payload configuration on Earth.
Launch the spacecraft and perform transfer to the Moon.
Insert the orbiter into lunar orbit, or deliver the lander to the surface (lander-mounted case only).
Commission the camera and operate it at the orbit altitude required for the intended ground scale.
For lander-mounted cameras, the camera bar position determines the view of the surface and rover; lander-side interfaces are not documented in the sources accessed.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Orbital terrain cameras are not deployed; they are fixed to the spacecraft and operated in orbit. The Chang'e-3 topography camera was mounted on a camera bar on top of the lander.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Orbiter examples: Chandrayaan-1 TMC, SELENE (Kaguya) TC, LRO NAC and Chandrayaan-2 TMC-2. Lander example: Chang'e-3 topography camera.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a specific lander, rover or spacecraft is asserted in this article. Such an assertion would require verified interface documents for the named vehicle.

article.historical_significance: The Chandrayaan-1 TMC was designed to produce a three-dimensional lunar atlas, and its data are archived through ISRO's ISSDC system [1][2]. The SELENE TC produced stereo images that were used in the SLDEM2013 global elevation mosaic, which JAXA states has an accuracy that no earlier whole-Moon dataset had reached [6]. LRO NAC stereo studies extended high-resolution topography analysis into targeted regions [8]. ISRO describes the Chandrayaan-2 TMC-2 as a smaller follow-on to the Chandrayaan-1 TMC, aimed at the same topographic products [3][4]. The Chang'e-3 topography camera supported local landing-area mapping and rover observation on the lunar surface [13][14].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties:
- **Chandrayaan-1 TMC in-flight performance.** The main TMC specification is from a pre-launch document [1]. The in-flight radiometric and geometric performance was not established from a primary post-mission source in this article.
- **SELENE TC stereo geometry and dates.** The stereo angle, mass, power and operating dates for the TC were not stated on the pages accessed. A secondary search summary gave a different stereo angle and was not used.
- **Henriksen et al. (2017).** The abstract was read through the USGS record. The full text was not read, so the slope statistics and mosaic results are taken from the abstract only [8][9].
- **LRO NAC band and mass limits.** The LROC pages do not state the NAC spectral band. The mass and power figures are per camera [10].
- **SDNDTM numerics.** The SDNDTM product has no numeric resolution or vertical accuracy on the help page accessed [11]. Its photometric-stereo products should not be read as geometric stereo DTMs.
- **Chandrayaan-2 TMC-2 status.** The ISRO pages describe the TMC-2 in general terms and do not state current operating status. The "Initial Results" page was not verified in full.
- **Chang'e-3 topography camera.** The abstract gives a field-of-view format and general role, but not the ground sampling distance, mass, power or spectral band. The full RAA paper [13] was not accessed.
- **Secondary claims excluded.** Several figures from search summaries, including a 40% mass and power reduction for TMC-2, a 0.4–0.9 µm band for an early Chandrayaan-1 TMC description and the detailed Kaguya stereo angle, were not verified against primary sources and are not used as values in this article.
- **Cross-references.** High-resolution imaging is covered under 027 (High-resolution camera), stereo imaging under 029 (Stereo camera), photogrammetry systems under 049 (Photogrammetry system) and digital terrain mapping systems under 050 (Digital terrain mapping system). This article does not duplicate those entries.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. Both registry images were verified to return HTTP 200 directly and to be listed on their JAXA source page. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery.

data_quality_notes: Chandrayaan-1 TMC specifications (band, 5 m resolution, 20 km swath, fore/aft angles, 6.3 kg, 370 x 220 x 414 mm) come from a pre-launch ISSDC configuration document. In-flight radiometric and geometric performance was not established from a primary post-mission source; the power figure is not published.

SELENE (Kaguya) TC stereo angle, mass, power and operating dates are not stated on the primary pages accessed (JAXA equipment page, ODE help page). A secondary search summary gave a stereo angle that conflicted with other summaries and was not used. The SLDEM2013 accuracy statement ('nearly 10 meters or better') is the publisher's own claim and was not independently re-derived.

Henriksen et al. (2017, Icarus) abstract was read through the USGS record; the full text was not read. The DOI resolves to Elsevier; the Icarus page was not fetched in full. LROC SDNDTM help page gives no numeric resolution or vertical accuracy.

Chang'e-3 topography camera: the RAA paper (Zhao et al. 2015, DOI 10.1088/1674-4527/15/11/010) was not accessed in full; the DOI returned a bot-protection page. Statements are abstract-level only. Ground sampling distance, mass, power and band are not publicly specified in the IAC-14 abstract accessed.

Chandrayaan-2 TMC-2 operational status, launch and operating dates were not verified from primary sources in this run; the ISRO payload page does not state current status. A catalogue-level 40% mass and power reduction claim was not verified and is not used numerically.

No image is included for Chandrayaan-1 TMC, LRO NAC, Chandrayaan-2 TMC-2 or Chang'e-3 topography camera because no direct asset URL was verified for them in this run; their source pages are cited in the Markdown article and reference list instead.
Image reuse conditions for JAXA website assets were not verified; check before republication.
